conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days, since becoming a mom can bring a huge mix of emotions and we want to be sure you’re supported. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through the questions one by one; each should only take a moment. When you’re ready, we can start.

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say as much as you always could, not quite as much, definitely not so much, or not at all?
I’d say… not quite as much. I still chuckle now and then, but it feels like it takes more effort, and most of the time I just don’t find much funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not quite as much… I can still laugh if something’s really silly, but it feels kind of forced, like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because it comes naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Definitely not as much as I used to. Even little things I used to get excited about—like a coffee outing or a show I liked—feel kind of flat. I still try to plan them, but the happy anticipation just isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I keep thinking it must be something I did—like I’m not feeding him right or holding him the “correct” way. Even tiny things, like dropping a burp cloth, make me feel like I’m failing at being a mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much every day. My mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenario—like if he sneezes I’m on high alert, sure it’s a sign of something serious. Even when he’s sleeping I’m checking to see if he’s breathing, and I can’t seem to shake the “what ifs,” even though I know most of them don’t make sense.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, it’s happened a few times this week. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath, like something awful is about to happen—even when the baby’s fine and the house is quiet. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… quite often. Sometimes the smallest tasks—folding a load of onesies or warming a bottle—feel like climbing a mountain. I’ll be standing in the kitchen with dishes everywhere and just freeze, thinking, “I can’t do all this,” even though I used to juggle way more before the baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, several nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through all the ways I’m probably messing up, and then I’m wide-awake listening to every little sound on the baby monitor. Even when I do drift off, I pop awake an hour later and can’t settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, really. It’s like this heavy cloud that settles over everything. I can still smile if someone talks to me, but inside I just feel empty and weepy, and sometimes I end up crying when I’m feeding the baby because it all feels so overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, that’s been happening. A few times this week it just hits me out of nowhere—I'll be folding his laundry or looking at his tiny socks and the tears start. I try to hide it so my older daughter doesn't see, but it feels like the sadness builds up until it spills over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t felt that. I do feel overwhelmed and down on myself, but I haven’t thought of hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy: laughter comes only with effort, activities you used to anticipate now feel flat, and most days carry a cloud of sadness that makes even folding tiny clothes end in tears. You describe near-constant worry about your baby's wellbeing, sudden panic spells, frequent self-blame, and nights spent unable to settle despite exhaustion. At the same time, you remain motivated to care for your children and have not had thoughts of harming yourself, strengths we want to build on.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient clearly states "Definitely not as much as I used to" and describes loss of pleasurable anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame for both significant and trivial events, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, daily anxiety with intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Clear description of unexpected panic attacks with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and inability to manage routine tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, repeated sleep disruption nearly every night tied to distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" with persistent heavy mood and frequent crying, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying "a few times this week" and describes unexpected tearful episodes, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 22 places you well above the 14-point cut-off that signals probable major <med>perinatal depression</med>. Your description of pervasive low mood, loss of interest, excessive guilt, recurrent panic, and sleep disruption lasting most of the day, nearly every day, aligns with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The combination of high anxiety and depressive symptoms warrants urgent assessment to differentiate depression with anxious features from a co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss whether an <med>antidepressant</med> might help
3. Share your EPDS results with a trusted family member so they can support follow-through with appointments and daily tasks
4. Prioritise 2-3 hour blocks of rest: accept help with overnight feeds, nap when the toddler naps, and practise brief breathing exercises before bed
5. Schedule a re-screen in one week; if suicidal thoughts develop, seek emergency care immediately
6. Continue checking in-progress is common and help is available
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery; exclusively parenting newborn and toddler.

Symptom Endorsement (EPDS-style items)
- Anhedonia: reduced laughter, little anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood: daily sadness, tearfulness multiple ×/wk  
- Sleep disturbance: initial & middle insomnia despite exhaustion  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Heightened anxiety: near-constant worry, intrusive “worst-case” thoughts, 2–3 panic spells this week  
- Feeling overwhelmed: routine tasks “freeze,” decreased coping  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negative)

Pattern  
Moderate–high distress across mood, anxiety, and functioning domains; symptoms present “most days” and coinciding with infant care demands.

Screening Significance  
Meets provisional cut-offs for possible major depressive episode with anxious features; rule-out perinatal anxiety disorder.  
Protective factor: denies self-harm; endorses motivation to “feel like me again.”

Next Steps  
1. Offer formal EPDS scoring & clinical interview at earliest opportunity.  
2. Provide psycho-education on perinatal mood/anxiety disorders.  
3. Discuss support resources (partner, family, home help).  
4. Re-screen within 1 week; immediate referral if suicidal ideation develops.
